dependency_coverage.name: setOf
dependency_coverage.meaning: Forms the set of all elements satisfying a predicate.
dependency_coverage.effect_on_target: Builds the event consisting of omega for which the finite sum of X i omega is at most epsilon times the number of indices.

binders: An arbitrary finite index type iota (possibly empty).
An arbitrary sample type Omega equipped with a measurable-space structure.
A measure mu on Omega, equipped with the assumption that it is a probability measure.
A family X indexed by iota, where each X_i is a real-valued function on Omega.
hypotheses: For every i in iota, X_i is measurable from Omega to the Borel real line.
The indexed family X satisfies ProbabilityTheory.iIndepFun X mu; this is the packet's indexed independence predicate with respect to mu.
For every i in iota, the function omega ↦ exp(-(1 / epsilon) * X_i(omega)) is mu-integrable.
For every i in iota, the mu-integral of omega ↦ exp(-(1 / epsilon) * X_i(omega)) is at most epsilon.
conclusions: Let n be the cardinality of iota. The real-valued mu-measure of the event {omega | sum over all i of X_i(omega) is at most epsilon * n} is at most (exp(1) * epsilon)^n.
mathematical_definitions: n = |iota| is a natural number, cast to a real number only in the threshold epsilon * n.
S(omega) = sum_{i in iota} X_i(omega) is the finite pointwise real sum.
exp(1) is the real number e, so the right-hand side is (e * epsilon)^n.
mu.real(A) is toReal(mu(A)); for a probability measure this represents the ordinary finite real probability of A.
translation.proposition_plain_english: For every finite (possibly empty) family of measurable real-valued random variables on a probability space and every positive real epsilon, if the family satisfies the packet's indexed independence predicate and each negative exponential transform exp(-X_i / epsilon) is integrable with expectation at most epsilon, then the probability that the sum of the variables is at most epsilon times the number of variables is at most (e * epsilon) raised to that number.

restrictions_and_vacuity_risks: The indexing type is finite but is not required to be nonempty. When it is empty, the event is all of Omega because 0 <= 0, and both sides of the conclusion equal 1 for a probability measure.
epsilon must be strictly positive; this in particular makes the reciprocal in the exponential well-defined and positive before negation.
The functions X_i are real-valued and Borel-measurable, and mu is specifically a probability measure.
No sign, boundedness, moment, or direct integrability assumption is imposed on X_i themselves; only their displayed negative exponential transforms are assumed integrable with bounded integrals.
The conclusion is a lower-tail bound with a non-strict pointwise threshold: sum_i X_i(omega) <= epsilon * |iota|.
For nonempty iota, if e * epsilon is at least 1, then the right-hand side is at least 1 and the probability bound may be automatically true and therefore uninformative.
The conclusion uses toReal(mu(A)); probability finiteness prevents the infinity-to-zero behavior of ENNReal.toReal from creating vacuity here.
No explicit measurability premise for the event is stated, although the finite sum of the assumed measurable real functions makes the displayed event measurable under standard meanings.
The exact internal definitions of the integral operator and indexed independence predicate are not fully exposed by the dossier, as recorded in the ambiguities.
ambiguities: D019 exposes MeasureTheory.integral only through an opaque wrapped projection. On the integrable functions in the hypotheses it is intended to be the usual Bochner/Lebesgue integral, but the dossier alone does not reveal its exact value on nonintegrable functions; that totalization does not affect this target because integrability is assumed.

D030 reduces iIndepFun to a Kernel.iIndepFun predicate whose definition is not included. Thus the exact formal independence condition cannot be reconstructed from the dossier alone, although its role is clearly an indexed independence assumption on the family X with respect to mu.
